questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Applying need-to-know during incident response
questions.performanceIndicator: Limit sensitive incident information while enabling each responder to perform assigned duties
questions.scenarioContext: A consumer electronics company is investigating suspected theft of unreleased product designs. Many employees ask to join the incident collaboration channel because rumors are spreading, but only a small cross-functional team has assigned response duties.
questions.prompt: How should access to incident details be managed?

choices.A: Grant access to all employees so the investigation appears transparent
choices.B: Provide role-specific information only to authorized participants with a defined operational need
choices.C: Restrict every detail to the lead investigator, including tasks required by technical responders
choices.D: Publish raw evidence internally after removing the incident title

questions.explanation: Need-to-know permits authorized responders to receive the information required for their roles while limiting unnecessary exposure of sensitive evidence and allegations. Organization-wide access is excessive, but withholding task-critical information from responders impedes the investigation. Removing a title does not make raw evidence safe for broad distribution.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Controlling emergency privileged accounts
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve emergency access while maintaining strong accountability and post-use review
questions.scenarioContext: A municipal services provider maintains a break-glass administrator account for use when the normal identity platform is unavailable. The password is currently known to several technicians and the account is excluded from monitoring.
questions.prompt: Which redesign would BEST protect the emergency capability?

choices.A: Keep the shared password unchanged so technicians can recall it during an outage
choices.B: Use the emergency account for routine maintenance to confirm that it still works
choices.C: Disable logging to prevent emergency activity from filling the monitoring system
choices.D: Secure the credential under controlled release, alert on use, record activity, and rotate it after each activation

questions.explanation: Controlled release, immediate alerting, activity records, and post-use rotation preserve emergency availability while maintaining accountability. A widely known static password invites misuse. Routine use defeats the exceptional purpose of the account, and disabling logging removes the evidence needed to review powerful emergency actions.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Reestablishing ownership and accountability for inherited assets
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply asset lifecycle controls after organizational change
questions.scenarioContext: After acquiring a smaller company, a publishing group discovers active servers, removable media, and network appliances that do not appear in either organization's asset records. Several systems have no identified business owner.
questions.prompt: What should operations management do FIRST?

choices.A: Inventory and reconcile the assets, assign accountable owners, and determine authorized disposition or continued use
choices.B: Connect every unidentified device to the production network to discover its purpose
choices.C: Discard all unrecorded equipment before checking for business data or retention obligations
choices.D: Allow local teams to retain devices indefinitely without central records

questions.explanation: Reconciliation and ownership assignment establish accountability before the organization decides whether each asset should remain in service, be isolated, or be disposed of under applicable data-handling rules. Connecting unknown devices increases risk. Immediate disposal may destroy needed data, while undocumented local retention perpetuates the control gap.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Preparing for eradication and controlled recovery after malware compromise
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify prerequisites that reduce reinfection and support trustworthy service restoration
questions.scenarioContext: A hotel chain has contained malware on a reservation server. Analysts found persistence mechanisms, stolen service credentials, and communication with several internal hosts. Management wants to return the server to production quickly.
questions.prompt: Which THREE actions should be completed before or as part of controlled recovery? Select 3 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Remove persistence or rebuild from a trusted source and verify the result
choices.B: Reconnect the server before investigating potentially affected internal hosts
choices.C: Rotate compromised credentials and review dependent services
choices.D: Preserve the pre-recovery logs and evidence required by the response process
choices.E: Restore the last available backup without determining whether it contains the compromise

questions.explanation: Trustworthy recovery requires removing persistence or rebuilding from a known-good source, replacing exposed credentials, and preserving evidence needed for investigation and reporting. Reconnection before checking related hosts can enable reinfection. A backup must be validated against the compromise timeline rather than restored solely because it is the newest copy.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Using sandboxing to analyze suspicious content
questions.performanceIndicator: Select an isolation control that supports behavioral analysis without exposing production endpoints
questions.scenarioContext: A legal services firm receives document attachments that evade signature-based anti-malware checks. Analysts need to observe file behavior before allowing the attachments onto user workstations.
questions.prompt: Which control BEST meets the requirement?

choices.A: Open each attachment on an analyst's normal workstation with local administrator rights
choices.B: Add every attachment sender to a permanent network blocklist
choices.C: Detonate the attachments in an isolated sandbox and evaluate their behavior and indicators
choices.D: Disable attachment inspection so documents arrive without processing delays

questions.explanation: An isolated sandbox allows analysts to observe process, file, and network behavior while reducing risk to production systems. Opening files on an ordinary privileged workstation creates exposure. Blocking every sender is overly broad and may not stop altered delivery methods, while disabling inspection removes a useful preventive and detective layer.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Managing rapidly changing malicious indicators
questions.performanceIndicator: Use time-bound blocking and monitoring without creating uncontrolled operational impact
questions.scenarioContext: A media streaming company receives credible indicators for command-and-control addresses used in an active campaign. Some addresses are hosted on shared infrastructure that also serves legitimate customers.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST operational response?

choices.A: Permanently block every address associated with the hosting provider
choices.B: Validate context, apply scoped time-bound blocks where justified, monitor effects, and review the indicators
choices.C: Ignore all network indicators because shared hosting can create false positives
choices.D: Replace existing firewall policy with the external indicator list without approval

questions.explanation: Context-aware, scoped, time-limited blocking can reduce active risk while monitoring and review limit harm to legitimate services as indicators age. Provider-wide permanent blocking is disproportionate. Ignoring credible intelligence forfeits protection, and replacing policy wholesale bypasses governance and can cause extensive disruption.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Governing a temporary patch exception
questions.performanceIndicator: Maintain accountability and risk reduction when immediate patching is not operationally possible
questions.scenarioContext: A diagnostic imaging system cannot accept a security patch until a compatibility review is completed. The vulnerability is relevant to the system, but network segmentation and strict administrative access can reduce exposure during the review period.
questions.prompt: How should the security manager handle the delayed patch?

choices.A: Close the vulnerability record because compensating controls are available
choices.B: Install the patch immediately without clinical or technical review
choices.C: Leave the system unchanged and omit the issue from risk reporting
choices.D: Approve a time-limited exception with compensating controls, ownership, monitoring, and a remediation date

questions.explanation: A time-limited, owned exception keeps the risk visible while compensating controls reduce exposure and compatibility work proceeds toward a defined remediation date. Closing or omitting the issue hides residual risk. Unreviewed installation may impair a safety-sensitive system and is not justified when controlled interim protection is feasible.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Tuning intrusion prevention without weakening detection
questions.performanceIndicator: Reduce false-positive disruption through evidence-based staged changes
questions.scenarioContext: An online education provider's intrusion prevention system repeatedly blocks legitimate enrollment traffic after a new signature update. The same signature may still detect a meaningful attack pattern elsewhere in the environment.
questions.prompt: Which response BEST balances protection and availability?

choices.A: Confirm the false-positive pattern, narrow or stage the rule for affected traffic, and monitor the revised control
choices.B: Disable the entire intrusion prevention platform across the enterprise
choices.C: Accept the enrollment failures because prevention rules should not be adjusted
choices.D: Exclude all enrollment systems from security monitoring

questions.explanation: Evidence-based tuning can preserve the signature's value while removing the specific condition that disrupts legitimate enrollment traffic; staged deployment and monitoring verify the result. Disabling the platform or excluding systems sacrifices broad protection. Accepting known business disruption without analysis fails to manage availability.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Selecting a recovery site for a moderate recovery time objective
questions.performanceIndicator: Match site readiness and cost to documented recovery requirements
questions.scenarioContext: A wholesale distributor must restore its inventory system within 12 hours after losing the primary facility. The organization can tolerate several hours of configuration and data restoration but cannot wait for new hardware to be purchased and delivered. A continuously synchronized duplicate environment exceeds the approved budget.
questions.prompt: Which recovery site is the BEST fit?

choices.A: A cold site containing office space and utilities but no installed computing equipment
choices.B: A warm site with installed infrastructure that requires configuration and data restoration
choices.C: A mirrored site with continuously synchronized processing and immediate failover
choices.D: A vacant warehouse selected only after the disruption occurs

questions.explanation: A warm site provides installed infrastructure and can be activated through configuration and restoration within a moderate recovery window, without the cost of continuous mirroring. A cold site may take too long because equipment must be obtained or installed. A mirrored site exceeds the stated need and budget, while an unprepared warehouse is not a viable recovery site.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Choosing a trustworthy restore point after data corruption
questions.performanceIndicator: Use integrity evidence and incident timing to prevent restoration of damaged data
questions.scenarioContext: A design firm's project repository has been silently corrupted for several days. Recent backups completed successfully, but completion status alone does not show whether the copied data was already damaged.
questions.prompt: What should the recovery team do before restoring production?

choices.A: Restore the newest backup because its job completed without an error
choices.B: Combine files from several backups without preserving their original versions
choices.C: Determine the corruption window, validate candidate backups, and restore the newest verified clean point
choices.D: Delete older backups so the team cannot select an outdated copy

questions.explanation: The team should identify when corruption began and validate backup contents and integrity before selecting the newest clean recovery point. Successful job completion proves that data was copied, not that it was sound. Combining versions without control can spread corruption, and deleting older copies removes potentially valid restore options.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Prioritizing recovery traffic with quality of service
questions.performanceIndicator: Preserve critical communications when disaster recovery operations share constrained network capacity
questions.scenarioContext: After a regional outage, a nonprofit's alternate site has limited network capacity. Voice coordination, identity services, database replication, and large noncritical software downloads compete for the same link, degrading critical recovery activity.
questions.prompt: Which measure would MOST directly improve recovery performance?

choices.A: Increase the retention period for network device configuration logs
choices.B: Route every traffic class with equal priority during the outage
choices.C: Suspend monitoring until all systems have returned to the primary site
choices.D: Apply tested quality-of-service priorities aligned with critical recovery functions

questions.explanation: Tested quality-of-service policies can prioritize voice, identity, and essential replication over noncritical downloads when capacity is constrained. Longer log retention does not allocate bandwidth. Equal treatment permits low-priority transfers to impair recovery, while suspending monitoring reduces visibility during a high-risk period.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Conducting a disaster recovery walkthrough
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize the collaborative review activities and outputs of a walkthrough exercise
questions.scenarioContext: A credit union has revised its disaster recovery plan and wants process owners to review their responsibilities together, trace the response to a presented outage, and identify missing dependencies without activating recovery systems.
questions.prompt: Which THREE activities belong in this walkthrough? Select 3 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Participants discuss the sequence of actions and handoffs for the presented event
choices.B: Production services are shut down and fully transferred to the alternate site
choices.C: Teams compare contact, resource, vendor, and dependency information against current conditions
choices.D: Facilitators record gaps, owners, and follow-up actions identified during discussion
choices.E: Recovered systems process live member transactions throughout the exercise

questions.explanation: A walkthrough is a collaborative, discussion-based review of plan steps, responsibilities, handoffs, and dependencies, with findings captured for correction. It does not require production shutdown or live transaction processing; those activities introduce operational testing beyond the stated objective.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Improving layered perimeter intrusion detection
questions.performanceIndicator: Integrate deterrence, detection, assessment, and response at a physical boundary
questions.scenarioContext: A remote telecommunications facility has a perimeter fence and locked equipment building. After several nighttime intrusion attempts, responders report that alarms do not show where entry was attempted and poor lighting prevents camera operators from assessing events.
questions.prompt: Which combination of safeguards would most directly enable responders to locate and assess a perimeter breach?

choices.A: Raise the interior office partition walls without changing perimeter monitoring
choices.B: Replace the equipment locks while leaving alarms and assessment capability unchanged
choices.C: Add zoned intrusion sensors, suitable lighting, camera coverage, and documented response procedures
choices.D: Post the alarm schedule publicly so nearby residents can investigate events

questions.explanation: Zoned sensors identify the event location, lighting and cameras support rapid assessment, and response procedures turn detection into action. Stronger interior partitions or locks may delay entry but do not correct poor alarm localization and assessment. Publicly assigning investigation to residents is unsafe and bypasses controlled response.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Selecting protective action during an external hazardous-material event
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize personnel safety using emergency authority and site-specific procedures
questions.scenarioContext: Authorities report an airborne chemical release near a call center and instruct nearby facilities to shelter in place. The building has designated interior refuge areas and a procedure for shutting down outside-air intake.
questions.prompt: What should the site emergency coordinator do FIRST?

choices.A: Activate the shelter-in-place procedure, account for occupants, and follow official emergency instructions
choices.B: Send all occupants outside to the parking area for a standard fire-drill muster
choices.C: Keep exterior doors open so employees arriving late can enter quickly
choices.D: Wait for visible symptoms before communicating with personnel

questions.explanation: The coordinator should follow the competent authority's shelter instruction, use the prepared refuge and ventilation procedures, and account for occupants. Moving people outdoors could expose them to the release. Open doors can admit contaminated air, and delaying action until symptoms appear sacrifices preventive life-safety measures.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Preparing personnel to report workplace violence warning signs
questions.performanceIndicator: Establish safe, confidential escalation and response channels for personnel concerns
questions.scenarioContext: Employees at a distribution company report that they do not know how to raise concerns about threats or escalating aggressive behavior. Managers currently handle reports informally, and workers fear that their identities will be disclosed unnecessarily.
questions.prompt: What program would most effectively improve early reporting and safe escalation?

choices.A: Require employees to confront the person directly before making a report
choices.B: Provide training, confidential reporting paths, defined escalation, and coordinated safety response procedures
choices.C: Publish every report and reporter's identity to discourage unsupported concerns
choices.D: Treat aggressive behavior solely as an information technology issue

questions.explanation: Training and confidential reporting, supported by defined escalation and coordinated response, help personnel raise concerns early without requiring unsafe confrontation or needless disclosure. Publishing identities can deter valid reports and increase risk. Workplace violence requires organizational safety coordination, not treatment as a purely technical matter.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Embedding security acceptance criteria in Agile delivery
questions.performanceIndicator: Integrate verifiable security conditions into backlog items and completion criteria
questions.scenarioContext: A digital publishing team uses short Agile iterations. Security defects recur because user stories describe business behavior but do not state security conditions, and completed stories are accepted after functional testing alone.
questions.prompt: Which change would BEST integrate security into the team's normal delivery process?

choices.A: Create a separate security backlog that is reviewed only before major releases.
choices.B: Add risk-based security acceptance criteria to applicable stories and include their verification in the Definition of Done.
choices.C: Ask the security team to rewrite every user story after developers complete the iteration.
choices.D: Permit product owners to accept stories with unresolved security criteria whenever functional objectives are met.

questions.explanation: Security acceptance criteria attached to relevant stories make expected controls testable, while the Definition of Done prevents work from being considered complete before those criteria are verified. A separate late backlog delays risk treatment. Rewriting completed stories creates rework, and accepting unresolved criteria based only on functionality allows known security gaps to accumulate.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Applying the Learning phase of the IDEAL improvement model
questions.performanceIndicator: Use measured pilot outcomes and lessons learned to refine the next improvement cycle
questions.scenarioContext: A property management company has completed a pilot of a new secure code-review process. Metrics show fewer escaped defects, but reviewers report that the approval workflow caused unnecessary delays for low-risk changes.
questions.prompt: What should the process improvement lead do NEXT?

choices.A: Expand the pilot unchanged because the defect metric improved.
choices.B: Discard the process because one part of the workflow created delays.
choices.C: Begin an unrelated tooling initiative before documenting the pilot results.
choices.D: Analyze the outcomes and lessons, refine the risk-based workflow, and feed the findings into the next improvement cycle.

questions.explanation: The Learning phase uses measured results and practical lessons to improve future cycles and institutionalize what worked. Expanding the process unchanged ignores the delay evidence, while abandoning it ignores the demonstrated reduction in escaped defects. Starting another initiative before capturing lessons wastes the pilot's evidence and weakens continuous improvement.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Planning security regression testing for maintenance updates
questions.performanceIndicator: Validate affected controls when a maintenance change alters shared application behavior
questions.scenarioContext: A hospital application team must upgrade a shared web framework to correct a security flaw. The framework also handles session management and request routing, and the application has extensive custom authorization logic.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST testing approach before production deployment?

choices.A: Perform risk-based regression and security testing focused on affected framework behavior and dependent controls, while retaining a tested rollback plan.
choices.B: Test only the original framework flaw because vendor maintenance releases do not affect application behavior outside the documented fix.
choices.C: Repeat only end-user functional tests because successful navigation demonstrates that authorization remains effective.
choices.D: Deploy the update directly to production and use incident monitoring as the primary validation method.

questions.explanation: The shared framework affects sessions, routing, and custom authorization dependencies, so testing should cover the corrected flaw and the security-sensitive behavior most likely to regress. Testing only the published defect assumes away integration effects. Functional navigation does not fully validate authorization, and production monitoring is not a substitute for predeployment assurance and rollback readiness.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Enforcing separation of duties in software release management
questions.performanceIndicator: Prevent one individual from developing, approving, and deploying the same change without oversight
questions.scenarioContext: At a small investment advisory firm, senior developers can write a change, approve their own review request, and deploy it to production. Management wants stronger control without requiring a large new release department.
questions.prompt: Which control would MOST appropriately address the risk?

choices.A: Allow self-approval for developers who have worked at the firm for more than one year.
choices.B: Rely on quarterly log review to identify improper deployments after they occur.
choices.C: Require independent approval for protected changes and restrict production deployment authority through the release workflow.
choices.D: Give all developers production access so responsibility for deployments is shared across the team.

questions.explanation: Independent approval and controlled deployment permissions introduce separation of duties at the critical approval and release points without requiring a large organization. Tenure does not remove conflict of interest. Quarterly review is detective and delayed, while broader production access increases rather than reduces the opportunity for unauthorized change.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Feeding operational security evidence back into software development
questions.performanceIndicator: Use production observations to drive prioritized lifecycle improvements
questions.scenarioContext: A subscription service releases frequently, but development planning relies almost entirely on feature requests. Operations has identified recurring application attack patterns and repeated control failures that are corrected individually but rarely influence future design work.
questions.prompt: Which TWO practices would BEST create an effective feedback loop into the SDLC? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Translate recurring production findings and attack patterns into prioritized backlog items, design guidance, and security requirements.
choices.B: Keep operational findings outside the development process so feature estimates remain stable.
choices.C: Measure development performance only by deployment frequency, regardless of recurring security failures.
choices.D: Close each incident record after service restoration without analyzing common software causes.
choices.E: Review trends across incidents, vulnerabilities, and control telemetry with development and product stakeholders at defined intervals.

questions.explanation: Operational evidence improves software security when recurring patterns become prioritized development work and when cross-functional trend reviews influence requirements and design. Isolating findings prevents learning. Deployment frequency alone can conceal recurring weaknesses, and closing incidents without analyzing common causes treats symptoms without improving the lifecycle.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Preventing directory traversal in file retrieval code
questions.performanceIndicator: Constrain file access to authorized resources after canonical path resolution
questions.scenarioContext: A legal document portal builds file-system paths by appending a client-supplied filename to a document directory. A tester uses encoded parent-directory sequences to retrieve a configuration file outside the intended location.
questions.prompt: Which remediation BEST addresses the underlying weakness?

choices.A: Reject only requests containing the literal sequence ../ before decoding the filename.
choices.B: Hide the document directory name and return a generic error for failed downloads.
choices.C: Encrypt configuration files while continuing to construct paths from client-supplied filenames.
choices.D: Map opaque identifiers to approved files server-side, canonicalize the resolved path, and verify it remains within the authorized directory.

questions.explanation: Server-side identifier mapping plus canonicalization and boundary validation prevents alternate encodings and path normalization tricks from escaping the authorized directory. A literal block rule can be bypassed. Hiding names does not enforce access, and encryption may protect some file contents but leaves arbitrary file retrieval possible.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Reducing risk from deserialization of untrusted data
questions.performanceIndicator: Replace unsafe object reconstruction with constrained data parsing and validation
questions.scenarioContext: A workflow application accepts serialized objects from partner systems and reconstructs application classes automatically. Security testing shows that crafted input can invoke unexpected class behavior during deserialization.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST design-level correction?

choices.A: Base64-encode serialized objects so class names are not visible during transmission.
choices.B: Use a simple data format with an explicit schema, validate permitted fields and types, and avoid automatic instantiation of arbitrary classes.
choices.C: Retain native object deserialization but log the class name after each object has been created.
choices.D: Compress serialized input before processing to reduce the opportunity for modification.

questions.explanation: Schema-constrained data parsing treats input as data and prevents untrusted content from selecting or instantiating arbitrary application classes. Encoding and compression change representation but not dangerous behavior. Logging after object creation may aid detection, yet execution may already have occurred and the unsafe design remains.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Preventing integer overflow in allocation calculations
questions.performanceIndicator: Validate numeric ranges and arithmetic before using calculated sizes
questions.scenarioContext: An image-processing service multiplies an uploaded image's width, height, and bytes per pixel to calculate a memory allocation. Very large values can wrap the calculation to a smaller number before the service copies image data into the buffer.
questions.prompt: Which coding practice MOST directly prevents this condition?

choices.A: Perform the calculation first and compare the resulting buffer size with available memory.
choices.B: Increase the process memory limit so wrapped calculations are less likely to cause a failure.
choices.C: Validate dimensions against safe limits and use checked arithmetic that detects overflow before allocation and copying.
choices.D: Record failed image operations in a log and block the source address after repeated errors.

questions.explanation: Range validation and checked arithmetic detect an unsafe calculation before a truncated allocation can lead to an out-of-bounds copy. Examining only the wrapped result misses the overflow. Additional memory does not correct arithmetic behavior, and logging with source blocking is a detective response that does not remove the vulnerable code path.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Enforcing security policy for infrastructure-as-code changes
questions.performanceIndicator: Detect and block unsafe deployment configurations before promotion
questions.scenarioContext: A video streaming company provisions application environments from infrastructure-as-code templates. Several recent changes enabled privileged workloads and overly broad storage permissions, even though the application source code passed review.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would BEST prevent similar configuration defects from reaching production?

choices.A: Place templates under review and version control, evaluate them with policy-as-code checks in the pipeline, and block violations unless a governed exception is approved.
choices.B: Review cloud billing reports after deployment to identify environments likely to contain privileged workloads.
choices.C: Scan only the application source because infrastructure templates do not execute business logic.
choices.D: Permit deployment engineers to correct template settings manually in production without updating the source template.

questions.explanation: Versioned review and automated policy checks treat infrastructure configuration as part of the software delivery system and prevent prohibited settings before deployment. Billing reports do not validate security configuration. Source-only scanning misses infrastructure risk, and manual production corrections create drift while leaving the defective template unchanged.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Preventing dependency confusion in package resolution
questions.performanceIndicator: Ensure builds retrieve approved internal and external packages from controlled sources
questions.scenarioContext: A consulting firm's build system searches both an internal package store and a public registry. A public package with the same name as an internal component and a higher version number is selected automatically during a build.
questions.prompt: Which control strategy would MOST effectively reduce this supply-chain risk?

choices.A: Allow the build to select the highest available version and investigate only when compilation fails.
choices.B: Rename internal packages periodically so public publishers cannot predict their future names.
choices.C: Block public packages only when their descriptions contain the firm's name.
choices.D: Route dependencies through a controlled repository, reserve internal namespaces, and pin approved package sources and versions.

questions.explanation: A controlled repository with namespace protection and explicit source and version rules prevents a public package from silently taking precedence over an internal dependency. Highest-version selection creates the weakness. Periodic renaming is fragile, and description-based blocking does not reliably establish package identity or provenance.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Assessing a third-party application without source-code access
questions.performanceIndicator: Select runtime testing and supplier evidence appropriate to a black-box acquisition
questions.scenarioContext: A nonprofit organization is evaluating a hosted donor-management application. The supplier will not provide source code but permits testing of a dedicated preproduction tenant and can provide independent security assessment evidence.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST assurance approach before acquisition?

choices.A: Treat the absence of source access as proof that meaningful security assessment is impossible.
choices.B: Perform authorized risk-based dynamic testing of the tenant and evaluate current independent evidence, architecture information, and remediation practices.
choices.C: Run static analysis against the public login page and consider the resulting client-side findings a complete assessment.
choices.D: Rely on contract pricing and service availability targets as substitutes for application security evidence.

questions.explanation: When source is unavailable, authorized dynamic testing combined with credible independent evidence and supplier process information provides layered assurance about exposed behavior and governance. Lack of source limits some techniques but does not prevent assessment. Client-side static analysis is incomplete, while pricing and availability targets do not demonstrate application security effectiveness.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Protecting an API from malformed requests and resource exhaustion
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply request validation and consumption controls at appropriate API layers
questions.scenarioContext: A ticketing platform exposes an API to approved partners. Authenticated clients can submit deeply nested payloads and issue high-cost search requests fast enough to exhaust application worker capacity.
questions.prompt: Which TWO controls would MOST directly reduce these application-layer risks? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Increase worker capacity whenever request latency exceeds the target.
choices.B: Validate requests against a strict schema with limits on size, depth, fields, and query complexity.
choices.C: Use longer partner identifiers while retaining unrestricted request volume and payload structure.
choices.D: Encrypt API traffic with a stronger transport cipher while leaving resource consumption unconstrained.
choices.E: Enforce quotas and risk-appropriate rate or cost limits per authenticated client and operation.

questions.explanation: Strict schema and complexity limits reject malformed or excessively expensive payload structures, while client- and operation-aware quotas constrain repeated resource consumption. Additional capacity may delay exhaustion without controlling abusive work. Identifier length is unrelated, and transport encryption protects confidentiality and integrity in transit rather than application resource usage.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Evaluating the sustainability risk of an open-source component
questions.performanceIndicator: Assess project health, support options, and exit strategy before adoption
questions.scenarioContext: An educational software team wants to adopt an open-source authentication component. The code appears functional, but releases are infrequent, unresolved security reports are increasing, and only one maintainer remains active.
questions.prompt: What should the application security lead recommend?

choices.A: Approve the component because source availability ensures the community will correct future vulnerabilities.
choices.B: Reject all open-source software because maintenance risk exists only when code is publicly available.
choices.C: Assess maintainership, vulnerability response, dependency health, internal support capability, and replacement options before making a risk-based adoption decision.
choices.D: Adopt the component and postpone lifecycle analysis until the first security defect affects production.

questions.explanation: Open-source adoption should consider project health, response history, dependencies, the organization's ability to maintain or support the code, and an exit path. Source availability does not guarantee timely remediation. Rejecting all open source ignores risk differences among projects, while delaying analysis creates avoidable dependency and replacement risk.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Prioritizing application security testing by change risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Allocate testing depth according to exposure, criticality, and modified trust boundaries
questions.scenarioContext: A food delivery company cannot perform the same depth of manual security testing on every weekly release. One release changes only internal report formatting, while another modifies payment workflows and introduces a new external service integration.
questions.prompt: How should the security testing effort be allocated?

choices.A: Use risk-based testing that gives greater depth to the payment and integration changes while maintaining defined baseline checks for all releases.
choices.B: Apply identical manual testing hours to both releases so the process treats every code change uniformly.
choices.C: Test only the larger code change because line count is the most reliable indicator of security impact.
choices.D: Skip testing of previously assessed components even when new integrations alter their trust relationships.

questions.explanation: Risk-based allocation concentrates scarce manual effort where critical data, external exposure, and changed trust boundaries create greater potential impact, while baseline controls preserve minimum assurance elsewhere. Equal hours ignore material differences. Code size is a weak proxy for risk, and prior assessment does not cover new interactions that change a component's exposure.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Verifying the authenticity of acquired software updates
questions.performanceIndicator: Validate update provenance and integrity before controlled deployment
questions.scenarioContext: A construction company receives an urgent update notice for commercial project-management software. The message links to an unfamiliar download host, although the update version appears consistent with the supplier's naming convention.
questions.prompt: What should the software owner do FIRST?

choices.A: Install the update on one production workstation because the version name matches the existing product.
choices.B: Upload the package to a public analysis service before confirming whether the supplier released it.
choices.C: Forward the link to additional administrators and compare whether they receive the same file.
choices.D: Obtain the update through a trusted supplier channel and verify its digital signature or published integrity information before testing and deployment.

questions.explanation: Trusted distribution and cryptographic verification establish provenance and integrity before the package enters the test or production process. A familiar version name is not authentication. Sending an unverified proprietary package to a public service may create exposure, and agreement among recipients does not prove that the download is genuine.
